title: Force and Acceleration in Classical Mechanics
short_intro: Force is an external agency capable of changing the state of rest or uniform motion of a body, directly causing acceleration according to Newton's laws of motion. Acceleration quantifies the rate of change of velocity vector per unit time within an inertial or non-inertial reference frame.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Newton's laws of motion, linear acceleration, tension in strings, pulley systems, apparent weight in lifts, and basic conservation of linear momentum.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Motion in non-inertial frames, pseudoforces, central forces, variable mass systems (rocket propulsion), and Lagrangian formulation of equations of motion.

prerequisites: Vector algebra (addition, dot product, cross product, and differentiation of vectors)
Kinematics of particles (displacement, velocity, and acceleration definitions)

concept_notes.heading: Newton's First Law and Inertial Frames
bullets: Defines inertial reference frames as frames in which Newton's first law of motion holds true.
An object remains at rest or in uniform motion unless acted upon by an external net resultant force.
Provides the qualitative definition of force and establishes the concept of inertia as inherent mass.

concept_notes.heading: Newton's Second Law and Momentum
bullets: The rate of change of linear momentum of a body is directly proportional to the applied external force and takes place in the direction in which the force acts.
Mathematically expressed as F = dp/dt, which reduces to F = ma for a system of constant rest mass m.
Establishes the fundamental equation of motion for a particle in classical mechanics under both constant and variable forces.

concept_notes.heading: Newton's Third Law and Action-Reaction Pairs
bullets: To every action, there is always an equal and opposite reaction acting simultaneously on different bodies.
Internal forces within an isolated system cancel out vectorially, leading directly to the law of conservation of linear momentum.
Applies universally to contact forces, gravitational forces, and electromagnetic forces alike.

concept_notes.heading: Non-Inertial Frames and Pseudoforces
bullets: Frames accelerating with respect to an inertial frame are non-inertial frames where Newton's laws do not directly apply without modification.
A fictitious or pseudoforce equal to -ma_0 must be introduced, where a_0 is the acceleration of the frame.
Coriolis and centrifugal forces arise as standard pseudoforces in rotating coordinate frames.

derivations.title: Equation of Motion for Variable Mass Systems (Rocket Equation)
derivations.conditions: A rocket moving in a gravity-free space expelling exhaust gas at a constant relative velocity.
steps: Write the initial momentum of the rocket-gas system at time t: p(t) = m(v + dv).
Write the final momentum at time t + dt: p(t+dt) = (m - dm)(v + dv) + dm(v - v_rel), where v_rel is exhaust velocity relative to the rocket.
Equate the change in momentum dp to zero for an isolated system, leading to m dv = v_rel dm.
Integrate the resulting differential equation from initial mass m_0 to m and initial velocity v_0 to v.

derivations.title: Acceleration of Two Bodies Connected by a String over a Fixed Pulley (Atwood Machine)
derivations.conditions: Inextensible, massless string and frictionless, massless pulley.
steps: Write equations of motion for mass m_1 moving upwards: T - m_1 g = m_1 a.
Write equation of motion for mass m_2 moving downwards: m_2 g - T = m_2 a.
Add the two equations to eliminate the internal tension force T: (m_2 - m_1)g = (m_1 + m_2)a.
Solve for acceleration a and substitute back to find tension T.
derivations.result: a = \left(\frac{m_2 - m_1}{m_1 + m_2}\right)g \quad \text{and} \quad T = \frac{2m_1 m_2 g}{m_1 + m_2}

formula_sheet.name: Newton's Second Law
formula_sheet.variables: F = force, p = momentum, m = mass, a = acceleration
formula_sheet.conditions: Constant mass system in an inertial frame

formula_sheet.name: Impulse-Momentum Theorem
formula_sheet.equation_html: J = \int F dt = \Delta p = m(v_2 - v_1)
formula_sheet.variables: J = impulse, F = force, dt = time interval, p = momentum
formula_sheet.units: Newton-second (N s) or kg m s^{-1}
formula_sheet.conditions: Valid for finite and impulsive forces

formula_sheet.name: Apparent Weight in an Elevator
formula_sheet.variables: W' = apparent weight, m = mass, g = acceleration due to gravity, a = lift acceleration
formula_sheet.conditions: + for upward acceleration or downward deceleration, - for downward acceleration

formula_sheet.name: Tsiolkovsky Rocket Equation
formula_sheet.variables: dv = change in velocity, v_rel = exhaust velocity, m_0 = initial mass, m_f = final mass
formula_sheet.conditions: No external gravitational or drag forces present

formula_sheet.name: Centripetal Acceleration
formula_sheet.variables: a_c = centripetal acceleration, v = linear speed, r = radius, \omega = angular velocity

formula_sheet.name: Coriolis Acceleration
formula_sheet.variables: omega = angular velocity vector of rotating frame, v = velocity vector of particle in rotating frame
formula_sheet.conditions: Particle moving inside a rotating reference frame

formula_sheet.name: Centrifugal Force
formula_sheet.variables: m = mass, omega = angular velocity, r = position vector from axis of rotation
formula_sheet.conditions: Observed from a rotating non-inertial frame

formula_sheet.name: Force in Central Force Field
formula_sheet.variables: f(r) = function of distance r from the force center, r-hat = unit position vector
formula_sheet.conditions: Force is directed towards or away from a fixed center point

graphs_and_experiments.title: Force versus Acceleration Graph
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A straight line passing through the origin on a Cartesian plot with acceleration a on the x-axis and force F on the y-axis.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The slope of the linear curve represents the inertial mass (m) of the experimental body, verifying F = ma.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Direct conceptual questions regarding slope interpretation and proportionality.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Atwood Machine Acceleration vs Mass Difference
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Plot of system acceleration a on the y-axis against mass difference (m_2 - m_1) on the x-axis for constant total mass.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Yields a straight line whose gradient gives g / (m_1 + m_2), confirming Newton's second law dynamics.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Used in numerical graph analysis problems for PGT examinations.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Spring Balance Reading in Accelerated Lift
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Apparent weight W' plotted against upward acceleration a of the elevator.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Linear positive slope starting from mg at a = 0, illustrating linear increase of apparent weight with upward acceleration.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Problem-solving involving apparent weight variations in elevators.

solved_numericals.question: A body of mass 5 kg is acted upon by a force F = (3t^2 \hat{i} + 4t \hat{j}) N. Find the magnitude of its acceleration at t = 2 s.
solution_steps: Calculate force at t = 2 s: F = (3(2)^2 \hat{i} + 4(2) \hat{j}) = (12 \hat{i} + 8 \hat{j}) N.
Use Newton's second law to find acceleration: a = F / m = (12/5) \hat{i} + (8/5) \hat{j} = 2.4 \hat{i} + 1.6 \hat{j} m s^{-2}.
Calculate magnitude of acceleration: |a| = \sqrt{(2.4)^2 + (1.6)^2} = \sqrt{5.76 + 2.56} = \sqrt{8.32} m s^{-2} \approx 2.88 m s^{-2}.

solved_numericals.question: A rocket burns fuel at a constant rate of 10 kg s^{-1} and ejects gas with a relative speed of 2000 m s^{-1}. Calculate the thrust force exerted on the rocket.
solution_steps: Identify given parameters: dm/dt = 10 kg s^{-1}, v_rel = 2000 m s^{-1}.
Apply the thrust force formula: F_thrust = v_rel \left(\frac{dm}{dt}\right).

solved_numericals.question: An elevator of mass 500 kg is ascending with an upward acceleration of 2 m s^{-2}. Find the tension in the supporting cable. (Take g = 9.8 m s^{-2})
solution_steps: Write equation of motion for the elevator: T - mg = ma.
Rearrange for tension: T = m(g + a).

assumptions_and_limitations: Newton's laws of motion are valid strictly in inertial reference frames unless modified by pseudoforces in non-inertial frames.
Classical mechanics assumes particle speeds are much smaller than the speed of light in vacuum (v << c), where relativistic mass-energy variations can be neglected.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Force is always required to keep an object moving at a constant velocity.
common_misconceptions.correct: Force is required only to change the velocity (accelerate); a body in uniform motion requires zero net external force.
common_misconceptions.why: Friction and air resistance are opposing forces that must be balanced to maintain uniform motion, confusing everyday experience with idealized first-law conditions.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Action and reaction forces cancel each other out so net force is always zero.
common_misconceptions.correct: Action and reaction forces act on two different bodies, hence they never cancel each other out.
common_misconceptions.why: Cancellation applies only to forces acting on the same single body when evaluating equilibrium.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Centrifugal force is a real inward pulling force.
common_misconceptions.correct: Centrifugal force is a fictitious or pseudoforce experienced only in rotating non-inertial frames directed radially outwards.
common_misconceptions.why: Real forces in circular motion are purely centripetal, directed towards the center of curvature.

quick_revision: Force equals the time derivative of linear momentum: F = dp/dt.
Inertial frames obey Newton's laws directly without auxiliary pseudoforces.
Apparent weight in a lift moving upward with acceleration a is m(g + a).
Thrust on a variable mass rocket is given by v_rel (dm/dt).
